- Plan postoperative analgesia, thromboprophylaxis, breast-feeding issues where applicable and specific maternal/fetal observation. [2]

### Gestational stage, fetal considerations and non-obstetric surgery

- Untreated severe maternal pain and physiological stress are also relevant risks; there is no good rule that withholding analgesia makes pregnancy safer.
- Establish gestation, indication for surgery, maternal comorbidities, medication exposure, haemodynamic status and whether obstetric consultation/fetal assessment is needed.
- Prefer a well-supported, effective plan using paracetamol and suitable regional/local techniques when appropriate, with carefully titrated opioid rescue if clinically needed.
- The benefits and harms of NSAIDs vary by gestational age—particularly fetal renal/oligohydramnios concerns from around 20 weeks and ductal risk later—and should follow contemporary obstetric prescribing guidance rather than a blanket 'safe until third trimester' statement.
- Aspirin prescribed for an obstetric indication is a separate treatment and should not be stopped casually.

- Pregnant patients have increased aspiration and airway-management challenges in some settings, and neuraxial sympathectomy may cause maternal hypotension that threatens uteroplacental perfusion.
- Prevent and rapidly treat maternal hypoxaemia/hypotension; plan positioning, airway and fetal considerations appropriate to the gestation.
- In the postpartum/breastfeeding period, drug passage into breast milk, infant gestation/health and maternal opioid requirement alter choices; avoid codeine/tramadol in breastfeeding when guidance warns of variable active-metabolite exposure.
- A short-acting opioid, if required, should be prescribed at an appropriate dose/duration with infant monitoring instructions and specialist advice for complex cases.
- The obstetric set owns detailed labour/caesarean pathways; Set 15 requires an anatomically and pharmacologically safe acute pain plan.

## 10.4 Special-population choices that change management

- In older people, pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic vulnerability and incomplete pain communication interact.
- Slower clearance and greater CNS sensitivity favour smaller titrated opioid doses with longer reassessment intervals where clinically appropriate; renal impairment increases exposure to certain metabolites, constipation and urinary retention are common, and multimodal regimens can worsen confusion if sedating agents are added indiscriminately.
- A patient with dementia can still have severe pain: observed guarding, agitation or reduced mobility may be more informative than a numerical rating, and caregiver history supplies the baseline.
- Use frequent reorientation, hearing aids/glasses, sleep and hydration care, avoidance of unnecessary anticholinergics and timely mobilisation alongside effective analgesia.

- Delirium should prompt a search for infection, hypoxaemia, urinary retention, metabolic disorder, withdrawal, pain or drug toxicity.
- Neither undertreatment of severe pain nor oversedation with opioids/benzodiazepines is a valid 'delirium prevention strategy'.
- A regional technique can reduce systemic opioid need, but a hypotensive or motor-dense infusion may harm rehabilitation.
- New disorientation after a peripheral block is not automatically a local anaesthetic complication, nor is agitation proof of inadequate opioid dose; reassess physiology and cognition.
- If antipsychotic management is considered for danger/distress, Parkinson or Lewy body disease and QT/other adverse risks demand special care.

- During pregnancy, maternal stabilisation and effective analgesia take priority: gestation alters aspiration, ventilation, uterine/aortocaval physiology and pharmacological risk.
- Assess fetal status with obstetric input when relevant, but necessary surgery and treatment should not be denied because of an assumption that any anaesthetic is teratogenic.
- Paracetamol is often the first pharmacological choice; use carefully selected short-term opioids for severe pain when indicated, with maternal respiratory monitoring and an appropriate plan for later gestation/neonatal exposure.
- NSAID restrictions evolve with gestation (particularly after around 20 weeks and late pregnancy).
- Ensure a fracture block covers the entire painful territory but does not conceal evolving compartment syndrome; postpartum/breastfeeding counselling needs agent-specific information rather than broad bans based on pregnancy letters. [2]

items.title: 11. Psychosocial factors, non-pharmacological and complementary treatments
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO) + P3 MODERATE (2 parent LOs)
items.body:
Allocated outcomes: AT_PM 1.2 (P3) and AT_PM 1.4 (P3). All six named psychosocial components are required.

## 11.1 The pain experience is biological, psychological and social

- Nociception does not linearly predict reported pain.
- Attention, threat appraisal, learning, previous trauma, mood, sleep and perceived control alter descending facilitation/inhibition, autonomic arousal and behaviour.
- A clinician should take pain seriously while recognising these modifiable influences.
- **Psychological support and explanation complement analgesia** and treatment of the underlying condition; they are not substitutes for investigating a dangerous cause or an excuse to declare pain inauthentic.

| **Named curriculum element** | **How it changes presentation or management** |
|---|---|
| **Anxiety** | Catastrophic predictions, anticipatory hypervigilance and muscular tension can amplify pain; explain procedure, offer coping choices and treat anxiety without reflexively adding benzodiazepine to an opioid regimen |
| **Depression** | Can reduce motivation, sleep, reward processing and engagement; assess safety, existing medicines and interaction risks; address pain and mood in parallel |
| **Placebo/context effects** | Trust, expectation and therapeutic ritual can alter symptoms through endogenous pathways; use transparent positive framing, not deception or withdrawal of effective treatment |
| **Active versus passive coping** | Pacing, movement, relaxation, self-efficacy and goal setting promote rehabilitation; passive reliance or fear-avoidance may sustain disability; adapt support to ability and illness |
| **Illness behaviour** | The way pain is communicated and activity is limited reflects learning, culture, fear and social context; assess without labelling the patient as manipulative |
| **Compensation/third-party issues** | Financial/legal uncertainty, workplace relationships and adversarial processes may affect distress or recovery; correlations do not prove malingering and should not bias safety or analgesic care |

**Clinical conversation:**

- “The pain is real; I want to understand both the tissue injury and what makes it worse.
- Our goals are that you can breathe, sleep and move while keeping treatment safe.” Use an interpreter where needed, validate cultural preferences and consider trauma-informed approaches.
- The person experiencing pain is the primary source about its impact, but clinical assessment must remain curious about causes and treatment response. [3]

## 11.2 Psychological mechanisms in a difficult acute-pain consultation

- Suppose a patient reports severe pain after apparently uncomplicated surgery while objective tissue damage is modest.
- Consider both a missed complication and heightened threat appraisal, fear, poor sleep, prior difficult medical experiences or withdrawal from an established medicine.
- Anxiety may increase vigilance and sympathetic arousal
- Depression may impair sleep, energy and engagement with physiotherapy
- Negative expectation/nocebo responses may amplify symptoms, while supportive explanation can improve the perceived safety of mobilisation.
- These physiological and cognitive effects are genuine changes in pain experience, not evidence of dishonesty.

- Active coping includes graded movement, goal setting, pacing and patient-led strategies; passive coping may include fear-driven avoidance, but it often reflects distress, limited resources or repeated undertreatment rather than poor character.
- 'Illness behaviour' describes how symptoms are communicated and influence action, not an accusation.
- Compensation, employer or insurer disputes can affect stress and recovery; they cannot establish malingering.
- Use neutral language, ask what the patient fears movement will do, set short achievable functional goals, provide a consistent plan across teams and treat nociceptive and neuropathic drivers appropriately.
- Explain that placebos/nocebos are context and expectation effects and should be harnessed through truthful communication, not deceptive medication. [3]

### Translate psychological factors into clinical actions

- Anxiety increases attention to threat and anticipatory pain; first explain the operation's expected pain trajectory, give patients some control over treatment and introduce breathing/relaxation skills or a supported regional plan.
- Depression may impair sleep, activity and adherence; ask about usual treatment and suicidal distress when clinically indicated, review antidepressant–analgesic interactions and coordinate support without assuming the pain is 'psychogenic'.
- Expectations and placebo/nocebo effects arise from therapeutic context and communicated predictions; positive, truthful explanation can support analgesia, whereas frightening or dismissive language can worsen suffering.
- Do not use deception to exploit a placebo response.

- Active coping includes paced mobilisation, goal-setting and self-management; passive coping may mean excessive bed rest or waiting for repeated rescue doses without engaging in recovery.
- These are modifiable behaviours, not moral virtues or failings.
- Illness behaviour may reflect genuine distress, learned responses, cultural context, prior care and social pressures; validate the report while examining function and investigating red flags.
- Compensation or third-party issues may influence reporting and recovery context, but an association never proves malingering.
- Ask about work, housing, carers, communication, language and rehabilitation barriers; involve a multidisciplinary service when disability or distress persists.
- An examiner expects an explanation of how these factors modify management, not a list of six words. [2,3]

## 11.3 Evidence-based non-pharmacological analgesia

- **Education, reassurance and shared goals** reduce uncertainty and support mobilisation.
- **Cognitive-behavioural and relaxation approaches** can improve coping; simple breathing, guided imagery, mindfulness or music may help some people though effect size and durability are variable.
- **Physical treatments**—ice/cryotherapy for selected injuries, elevation/immobilisation where required, heat for appropriate muscle conditions, physiotherapy, graded mobilisation, positioning and sleep measures—have mechanistic roles and often low systemic toxicity.
- Avoid cold/heat where vascular insufficiency, sensory loss, burns or other injury makes it unsafe.
- Ask what worked previously and measure function, not just immediate satisfaction.

## 11.4 Complementary/alternative medicines: mechanism, clinical use and uncertainties

| **Intervention** | **Proposed mechanism / intended use** | **Evidence and safety interpretation** |
|---|---|---|
| **Acupuncture/electroacupuncture** | Somatosensory afferent stimulation and endogenous descending pain modulation; some postoperative and musculoskeletal settings | Modest, heterogeneous effects; requires sterile technique and informed consent, particularly around anticoagulation/infection |
| **TENS** | Large-fibre afferent stimulation, segmental gating and descending modulation; adjunct for selected musculoskeletal/postoperative pain | Benefit varies by condition, stimulation setting and treatment duration; not a substitute for source control; avoid unsafe electrode placement and consider implanted devices |
| **Hypnosis, guided imagery, mindfulness** | Attention, cognitive appraisal, autonomic arousal and expectation modulation | May support coping and lower distress; requires cooperation, no guaranteed reduction in opioid use |
| **Massage/manual therapy** | Tactile input, muscle relaxation and perceived control | Useful for selected muscular discomfort, but avoid over unstable fracture, thrombus, infection or vascular compromise |
| **Herbal supplements / cannabinoids** | Numerous proposed inflammatory, endocannabinoid or sedative pathways | Formulations and doses vary, evidence for routine acute perioperative benefit is poor; drug interactions, sedative effects, bleeding risk and product contamination are concerns |

- Do not equate complementary therapies with evidence-equivalent surgical analgesia; conversely, do not dismiss a low-risk technique that helps an individual patient meet functional goals.
- Ask explicitly about **St John’s wort** (enzyme induction, serotonergic interactions), **kava** (sedation/hepatic harm), herbal platelet-active products and cannabis/other products when assessing anaesthetic interactions.
- Record use respectfully. [2,3]

### Critical appraisal rather than automatic endorsement or dismissal

- Distinguish a plausible mechanism from convincing clinical benefit.
- **Acupuncture** may engage segmental nociceptive modulation, descending pathways and contextual effects; some trials show small short-term pain or opioid-sparing differences, but effects are condition-dependent, sham-controlled comparisons can be difficult and needle bleeding/infection matter in anticoagulation or immune suppression.
- **TENS** delivers cutaneous electrical stimulation, potentially engaging segmental gating and descending inhibition; it may be trialled for selected focal pain if the patient benefits, with appropriate device/pacemaker/skin precautions, but does not replace treatment of an acute surgical complication.
- **Heat/cold, massage and relaxation** may reduce spasm, swelling, anxiety or distress in appropriate cases, but are unsuitable over fresh ischaemic tissue, insensate skin or unstable fractures.

- Herbal products and supplements are often omitted from drug charts.
- Ask specifically about products, dose and last use: some have antiplatelet, sedative, sympathomimetic or serotonergic activity, inconsistent composition, uncertain interactions and contamination risks.
- Avoid presenting an unverified supplement as an evidence-based analgesic or claiming that 'natural' implies perioperative safety.
- For each therapy discuss proposed mechanism, indication, evidence quality and effect size, contraindications, patient preference, cost, implementation and an objective functional reassessment.
- The ethical position is an informed adjunctive trial when reasonable, not substitution for necessary analgesia, diagnosis or source control.

## 11.5 Complementary therapies: clinical application and critical appraisal

- Acupuncture and electroacupuncture stimulate sensory afferents and may engage spinal gating and descending endogenous opioid/monoaminergic mechanisms; trials in postoperative pain are heterogeneous and effect size depends on setting and controls.
- TENS applies cutaneous electrical stimulation and may engage large-fibre segmental inhibition and descending modulation; adequate intensity and electrode positioning matter, while patient selection includes skin integrity and device/implant precautions.
- Mindfulness, guided imagery, hypnosis and relaxation act on attention, cognitive threat appraisal and autonomic arousal and can support distress tolerance without replacing needed surgery or analgesia.
- Massage, positioning, movement and heat/cold address mechanical discomfort but can be unsafe over fractures, poor perfusion, neuropathic skin or active thrombotic disease.
- Herbal remedies and cannabis products require explicit medication reconciliation: contents and dose can vary, and antiplatelet, sedative, serotonergic, enzyme-inducing and hepatic interactions may be important.

- The correct ANZCA-style appraisal discusses putative mechanism, indication, evidence quality, plausible benefit, specific adverse effects and the patient's preferences.
- Complementary does not mean ineffective, harmless or interchangeable with established treatment.
- If an individual benefits without contraindication, incorporate the therapy as an adjunct and measure function; do not imply robust prevention of chronic pain or a major mortality benefit from low-certainty studies. [2,3]

items.title: 12. Palliative-care pain and pain management near the end of life
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO) + P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO)
items.body:
Allocated outcome: AT_PM 1.17 (P3); ANZCA PG67(G) 2022 and PS45 2025.

## 12.1 Start with the patient’s aims, not an automatic surgical or opioid pathway

- Palliative analgesia is guided by **goals of care, prognosis, reversibility of painful causes, comfort/function, ability to swallow, existing tolerance and the patient’s wishes**.
- Clarify decision-making capacity, advance-care documents, family and substitute decision-maker involvement where appropriate, and whether the procedure meaningfully improves comfort or creates disproportionate burden.
- Pain may be nociceptive, neuropathic, incident with movement, visceral/colicky or due to pressure injury, fracture or cancer.
- A distressing symptom requires prompt relief even when curative interventions are not appropriate; palliative care does not mean withholding capable treatment or indiscriminately sedating the patient. [3,4]

## 12.2 Design a flexible regimen and reassess often

- Continue effective baseline analgesia while ensuring an appropriate **breakthrough/rescue** route and dose; calculate opioid conversions carefully as organ function changes.
- If oral intake is unreliable, consider a subcutaneous infusion with breakthrough doses under the local palliative-care protocol; IV delivery may be necessary for rapidly unstable or severe symptoms.
- Treat reversible issues—constipation, retention, fracture instability, infection or neuropathic mechanisms—when consistent with goals.
- For neuropathic pain, a carefully selected adjuvant may be useful but can take time and cause unacceptable sedation if prognosis is short.
- Corticosteroids, radiotherapy, surgery or nerve block can help specific cancer-related syndromes, but benefits and procedural burdens must be discussed.
- Opioid neurotoxicity/myoclonus or delirium with renal failure may require agent rotation and dose review.
- The usual goal shifts from rehabilitation milestones to **relief of distress and preserved desired interaction**, with respect for patient choice.

- Distinguish **proportional symptom treatment** from intentional deep sedation: the latter requires a separate specialist ethical and clinical framework for refractory suffering.
- Discuss double-effect principles carefully and do not assume every opioid escalation hastens death.
- PG67 focuses on ethical perioperative decisions, communication and proportionality in people approaching end of life; it is not a drug dosing formulary. [4]

## 12.3 A practical end-of-life pain pathway for surgery and non-operative care

- Clarify the immediate aim: is the patient's overriding concern rest pain, predictable movement pain during wound care, dyspnoea, fear, or preserving alert conversation with family?
- Identify reversible burdens (urinary retention, pathological fracture, bowel obstruction, nerve compression, a poorly fitting device, constipation) and treat those where compatible with goals.
- Consent and decisions about procedures depend on capacity, patient values and any legal substitute decision-maker; reassess proportionality when the anticipated surgical burden exceeds the chance of relief.
- PG67 provides an ethical and communication framework for this choice, not an opioid dosing chart. [4]

- For stable oral intake, continue a proven baseline opioid where appropriate with short-acting rescue for breakthrough episodes, and document how rescue doses are reviewed against 24-hour use.
- For impaired swallowing, consider subcutaneous delivery or an alternate route under the specialist/local pathway; do not assume oral absorption or copy an IV conversion unchanged.
- Renal or hepatic failure may lead to metabolite accumulation, sedation or neurotoxicity and calls for careful selection/rotation.
- If pain is localised, consider short-course targeted radiotherapy, regional/neurolytic intervention or a surgical palliative procedure only when benefit, likely onset and procedural burden fit prognosis.
- Corticosteroids may help selected oedema/nerve-compression syndromes while adding delirium, hyperglycaemia or infection risk.
- Neuropathic drugs often need time to work, so for very limited prognosis rapid comfort measures are more important than a complicated long-term titration schedule.

- A patient near death may experience severe pain and breathlessness together.
- Opioids can relieve both when titrated to symptoms with careful assessment, but distressing agitation may also arise from delirium, hypoxia, withdrawal or urinary retention.
- Do not reflexively label every movement 'pain' or sedate solely because the family is distressed.
- Explain likely drug effects, monitoring appropriate to goals, breakthrough instructions, and whom to contact out of hours.
- Proportional symptom relief and palliative sedation for refractory suffering are different decisions with different safeguards and specialist involvement.
- Bereavement support and continuity across ward, hospice and community are part of good care. [3,4]

### Turn palliative principles into a prescribing and communication plan

- **Case: advanced intra-abdominal malignancy, deteriorating kidney function, partial obstruction and severe movement pain.** Clarify whether the patient wants wakeful interaction with family, rapid relief at rest, time at home, or a procedure to permit eating.
- Assess pain mechanism (visceral colic, peritoneal stretch, neuropathic infiltration, fracture) and reversible contributors (constipation, urinary retention, infection, obstruction).
- Discuss prognosis and burdens of further anaesthesia, interventional drainage, stent or surgery with the treating and palliative teams.
- If relief from a procedure is unlikely before life expectancy is exhausted, a non-operative approach may better respect goals; do not deny potentially useful procedures merely because care is palliative.

- Prescribing starts with a reliable estimate of current opioid exposure, including long-acting oral or transdermal medication, recent rescue doses, and the time course of pain.
- If oral absorption is unreliable, choose a suitable alternate route—often subcutaneous continuous infusion plus breakthrough doses under the local palliative protocol—and ensure the PRN dose is coordinated with the basal regimen.
- In severe rapidly changing pain, clinician-titrated parenteral opioid with close review may be needed; transdermal patches are less suitable for rapidly unstable requirements because their onset and offset are slow.
- Renal dysfunction may favour an alternative opioid or specialist rotation; methadone, fentanyl and high-dose conversions require expertise.
- Write orders for breakthrough pain, nausea, constipation and other likely adverse effects, and provide nursing instructions about signs of toxicity and how to request urgent review.
- NICE supports explicit communication, frequent review, breakthrough treatment and specialist advice in significant renal/hepatic impairment. [25]

- The assessment target depends on the patient's preferences.
- A patient who prioritises alert conversation may accept moderate discomfort during nonessential movement, while another may prefer more sedation to control otherwise intolerable symptoms.
- Distinguish pain from terminal agitation, delirium, dyspnoea or a distended bladder rather than reflexively doubling an opioid.
- When severe suffering persists despite proportionate measures, specialist assessment of whether symptoms are refractory and consideration of palliative sedation follow a separate ethical and clinical process; ordinary titration of analgesia to pain relief is not synonymous with intention to hasten death.
- Document goals, consent/capacity and communication with whānau/family, out-of-hours support, community supplies and next review.
- PG67 provides the perioperative end-of-life decision framework; it is not a dosing protocol. [4,25]

- **Exam synthesis:** establish the patient's goals; distinguish mechanisms; investigate/treat reversible burdens if consistent with goals; choose a feasible route and opioid/adjuvant with rescue; manage adverse effects and changing clearance; review function/comfort; coordinate multidisciplinary and community continuity.

items.title: 13. Enhanced recovery, rehabilitation and a return to function
items.priority: P1 CORE (2 parent LOs) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.body:
Allocated outcome: AT_PM 1.5 (P5), integrating the core planning outcomes.

- Effective acute pain management is an enabling component of enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS): it supports early breathing, feeding, mobilisation, sleep and participation in physiotherapy while minimising nausea, ileus, hypotension, urinary retention and excessive sedation.
- Procedure-specific **multimodal analgesia and motor-sparing regional techniques** are often preferable to large opioids, but no individual technique guarantees earlier discharge or elimination of chronic pain.
- If regional analgesia causes hypotension, quadriceps weakness or inability to mobilise safely, the apparent resting analgesia benefit may be outweighed by recovery harm. [6–8]

**Examples:**

- A patient after TKA benefits from an adductor canal block and surgeon local infiltration with regular paracetamol/appropriate NSAID, rescue opioid and early mobilisation; a motor-dense femoral block may undermine rehabilitation through quadriceps weakness.
- After open abdominal surgery, effective dynamic analgesia should allow cough and mobilisation without fluid overload/hypotension from a neuraxial infusion.
- After thoracic injury/surgery, analgesia should improve inspiratory volume and cough while preserving vigilance against OIVI.
- After ambulatory surgery, provide a short oral plan that patients can safely self-administer.
- Evaluate quality of recovery, function and patient-valued outcomes rather than a single lower pain score at one hour.

**Discharge from an acute pain service requires continuity:**

- Catheter removal according to anticoagulant timing, transition off PCA, review of opioids and sedation, bowel regimen, safe supply and taper instructions, communication to primary care and a plan for unexpectedly persistent pain.
- The aim is to avoid a poorly supervised transition from short-term postoperative opioid therapy to unnecessary long-term exposure. [2,13]

## 13.1 Evaluate ERAS outcomes, not only a pain-score intervention

- An ERAS pathway integrates preoperative education, adequate analgesia, early feeding/mobilisation, PONV prevention, appropriate fluid care and removal of unnecessary catheters.
- A pain intervention is valuable when it improves one or more patient-important recovery outcomes with acceptable harm.
- Evaluate ability to breathe/cough, transfer, walk, eat, participate in rehabilitation, length of stay, respiratory events, PONV, ileus, falls and satisfaction, rather than claiming that a lower 2-hour NRS automatically shortens admission.
- A dense femoral block after knee arthroplasty may reduce pain but hinder quadriceps strength and walking; a motor-sparing block plus infiltration and basic analgesia may better serve rehabilitation.
- An epidural after open abdominal surgery may improve dynamic analgesia but persistent hypotension can cause fluid loading and delayed mobilisation; the choice differs from minimally invasive surgery.
- A heavily sedating opioid-free combination may be less 'fast-track' than a modest balanced opioid regimen.

- Practical governance includes procedure-specific pathways, standard orders and rescue criteria, nurse/physiotherapist education, validated functional assessments, patient-centred discharge instructions, and auditing opioid exposure, unexpected admissions and adverse effects.
- Delayed recovery is not automatically due to analgesia: surgical complications, haemodynamic instability, baseline frailty and social circumstances also determine readiness. [2,6,7]

### Evaluating an ERAS or fast-track analgesic bundle

- A faster discharge is only a success if it is accompanied by safe pain control, mobilising ability, nutrition, sleep, reduced postoperative nausea, patient satisfaction and no excess readmissions.
- Multimodal analgesia contributes by reducing opioid-related ileus, sedation and nausea and enabling physiotherapy, but the most useful regimen is procedure-specific.
- A dense femoral block may lower knee pain but delay walking through quadriceps weakness; an effective adductor canal strategy may better support function.
- A high-dose neuraxial opioid may improve rest pain but create pruritus, urinary retention or prolonged respiratory monitoring requirements; analgesic choice must fit the intended pathway.

- When asked to evaluate an enhanced-recovery analgesic technique, state its proposed pathway (less noxious input/opioid exposure → earlier mobilisation and gut recovery), then the relevant evidence, comparator and harms.
- Monitor pain on movement, rescue opioid consumption, adverse effects, time to mobilisation/oral intake, length of stay and reattendance.
- Avoid claiming that every opioid-sparing difference translates into fewer complications or shorter admission; for example, the ALLEGRO trial found no routine gastrointestinal-recovery advantage from IV lidocaine after minimally invasive colon surgery.
- Service quality requires audit, staff training and a discharge protocol, not simply adding another infusion. [2,11]

items.title: 14. Clinical synthesis: turn the learning outcomes into an anaesthetic plan
items.priority: P1 CORE (6 parent LOs) + P5 MINIMUM (4 parent LOs)
items.los: BT_PM 1.32; IT_GS 1.14; IT_PM 1.7; IT_PM 1.8; AT_PM 1.13; IT_PM 1.13; AT_PM 1.5; AT_PM 1.15; IT_PM 1.14; AT_PM 1.6
items.body:
These cases are **teaching examples**, not invented past-examination questions. A good Final answer prioritises safety, demonstrates an appropriate sequence and links proposed therapy to examination findings and expected function.

## 14.1 Severe pain after outpatient laparoscopy — unexpected PACU pain

- A normally well 20-year-old has persistent NRS 9 pain despite local infiltration and multiple fentanyl boluses at a stand-alone day unit.
- **First assessment:** vital signs and sedation, surgical operation and unexpected events, wound and abdominal examination, shoulder-tip/gas pain versus peritonism, bleeding, bladder, nausea, prior analgesics and block detail.
- The working diagnosis is not automatically “opioid resistant”; deteriorating BP or a rigid abdomen demands immediate surgical review.
- **Immediate treatment:** reassure and reposition, ensure appropriate paracetamol and anti-inflammatory therapy if safe, titrate monitored IV opioid, antiemetic and consider local/regional rescue as indicated; reassess function and breathing after each step.
- **Disposition:** if ongoing IV/PCA, surgical intervention or overnight observation is needed, arrange transfer to a named receiving hospital and monitored transport.
- Provide an oral plan only once pain is manageable, the cause assessed and discharge criteria satisfied.

## 14.2 Older patient with hip fracture and dementia

- An 83-year-old with dementia cannot explain the pain score and is distressed with every movement.
- Assess baseline behaviour, observational pain cues, fracture and limb perfusion, medications/renal function and delirium triggers.
- Give a fascia iliaca block or other suitable hip regional analgesia as soon as feasible; prescribe adjusted regular paracetamol and small monitored opioid rescue; consider NSAID only after assessing kidney/GI/bleeding risks.
- Protect orientation, sleep, hearing/vision and family support.
- Recheck pain with transfers and mobilisation, bowel care, ventilation, confusion and need for additional rescue.
- **The exam distinction:** undertreatment of pain and oversedation can both worsen delirium.

## 14.3 Drowsy patient on postoperative morphine PCA

- A 68-year-old with OSA receives oxygen and PCA; he is difficult to rouse, snores intermittently, RR 6/min and SpO₂ 96%.
- Treat as life-threatening OIVI despite an apparently satisfactory pulse oximeter.
- Stop opioid delivery and co-sedatives, call for help, support airway and ventilation and give titrated naloxone as needed; investigate other causes and monitor for renarcotisation.
- Review the original prescription, pump programming, recent sedatives, kidney function, overnight observations and whether a regional/non-opioid alternative is safer.
- **Do not wait for desaturation and do not let naloxone replace ventilation.** [5]

## 14.4 Profound hypotension with a thoracic epidural

- On the evening after open abdominal surgery, a patient receiving epidural ropivacaine/fentanyl develops MAP 48 mmHg. First assess consciousness, perfusion, oxygenation, rhythm, catheter recent bolus and sensory level while urgently excluding haemorrhage and sepsis.
- Pause epidural local anaesthetic, summon senior help, use targeted vasopressors, and give carefully assessed fluid only when deficits/responsiveness are credible.
- Review whether excessive segmental block, cardiac dysfunction or blood loss dominates.
- Once stable, assess dynamic pain and consider restarting at a lower effective infusion or substituting PCA/plane-block analgesia.
- If new leg weakness/back pain occurs, activate the neuraxial compressive lesion pathway and urgent imaging rather than reassuring yourself it is “just the epidural.”

## 14.5 After spinal anaesthesia, ascending weakness and apnoea

- A patient becomes nauseated, severely hypotensive and bradycardic, then cannot lift arms or breathe adequately after an intended neuraxial block.
- The sequence is **high/total spinal until proven otherwise:** call for assistance, stop dosing, deliver oxygen and effective positive-pressure ventilation/intubation when required, treat hypotension and bradycardia immediately, support circulation with vasoactive drugs and full ALS if arrest occurs.
- Reassess other causes including LAST, anaphylaxis, haemorrhage or catastrophic neuraxial complication.
- Keep airway and haemodynamic support until the block regresses; in pregnancy, coordinate uterine displacement and maternal resuscitative delivery decisions with the obstetric team.

## 14.6 Multi-rib trauma with progressive oxygen requirement

- A 75-year-old with five lateral fractures, COPD and painful coughing uses escalating morphine but cannot inspire deeply.
- Assess fracture/contusion and pleural injury, infection and respiratory failure; document inspiratory effort, cough and repeated respiratory assessment.
- Provide regular systemic non-opioids where safe, small opioid rescue, lung expansion and early regional referral.
- A unilateral ESP/SAP or paravertebral catheter may improve cough while limiting systemic sedation; a thoracic epidural may be useful but hypotension, anticoagulation and concurrent injuries must be assessed.
- Anticipate pulmonary complications, frequent reassessment and escalation if ventilation worsens.
- **Analgesic success is restored cough and ventilation, not simply rest NRS 2.** [18]

## 14.7 Sickle pain episode with new hypoxaemia

- A 27-year-old with known sickle cell disease presents with severe back/limb pain and later fever and SpO₂ 89%.
- Give rapid pain assessment and timely **individualised** opioid treatment with reassessment, non-opioid adjuncts and careful fluid replacement only if clinically dehydrated.
- Investigate acute chest syndrome immediately; give oxygen for hypoxaemia and involve haematology for transfusion decisions.
- Do not dismiss severe reported pain as drug seeking, force routine large-volume IV fluids, or transfuse uncomplicated pain episodes indiscriminately. [15]

## 14.8 A day-one TKA patient with weak quadriceps

- The patient reports good resting pain control but cannot safely stand after a dense femoral nerve block.
- Assess motor power, local anaesthetic exposure, surgical neurological status, fall risk and expected recovery; review whether a more motor-sparing technique would support rehabilitation.
- A contemporary TKA package typically includes scheduled paracetamol and NSAID/COX-2 if safe, **adductor canal block plus periarticular infiltration**, appropriate perioperative dexamethasone and opioid rescue.
- Intrathecal morphine has a limited incremental role when robust regional/infiltration is already used and adds delayed monitoring requirements. [6,7]

## 14.9 Worked integrated case: opioid-tolerant patient with OSA and a major incision

- A 55-year-old is scheduled for open abdominal surgery, has OSA on CPAP, stage 3 CKD and uses verified maintenance buprenorphine for opioid-use disorder.
- PREOPERATIVE: determine baseline regimen and last dose, actual analgesic tolerance, co-prescribed sedatives, prior acute pain responses, respiratory monitoring resources and the anticipated incision.
- Involve the maintenance prescriber and acute pain service early; continuation of buprenorphine with a co-ordinated acute analgesia plan is commonly appropriate, rather than unplanned cessation.
- Explain that more medication may be required for acute nociception but monitoring and regional treatment remain essential.
- Discuss a thoracic epidural or suitable abdominal wall block after checking anticoagulation, haemodynamics and expected recovery.

- INTRAOPERATIVE: ensure paracetamol (appropriately adjusted if low weight/liver concerns), select anti-inflammatory therapy cautiously given CKD and operative anatomy, add an effective incision-matched local/regional technique if safe, and provide titrated opioid or specialist ketamine adjunct if needed; a sole 'opioid-free' approach that leaves uncontrolled pain at emergence is not an acceptable objective.
- POSTOPERATIVE: prescribe a monitored rescue strategy, usually with acute pain service oversight; if PCA is selected, explicitly define drug, concentration, demand dose, lockout, basal-rate rationale and sedation/ventilation observations.
- Avoid a basal infusion by habit, combine with CPAP and enhanced monitoring according to risk, and never rely on saturation alone.
- Check cough, transfer and movement and treat nausea/constipation.
- DISCHARGE: reconcile ongoing buprenorphine, cease hospital-only rescue, plan return to the patient's established regimen with a time-limited short-acting opioid only if still needed, and communicate with their usual prescriber.
- This demonstrates why pain aetiology, drug pharmacology, dependence, organ function and airway risk must be integrated rather than addressed as separate lists.

items.title: 15. Landmark evidence and how to use it in the Final
items.los: Integrates the outcomes in this set
items.body:
Do not memorise trials as slogans. State the **population, comparison, outcome, direction, uncertainty and what cannot be extrapolated**.

| **Evidence** | **What it established** | **Limitations and exam application** |
|---|---|---|
| **ANZCA PS41(G) 2023 [2]** | Acute pain requires individualised assessment, skilled service delivery, multimodal analgesia, repeated efficacy/adverse-effect review and stewardship across admission/discharge | College position statement, not a universal dose or surgical procedure algorithm |
| **ANZCA PS45 2025 [3]** | Respectful equitable, patient-centred pain management and clinician duties to identify and address barriers | A right to care does not establish that every proposed modality is evidence-effective |
| **Jansen & Dahan, BJA Education 2024 [5]** | μ-opioid depression of breathing, upper airway and arousal; risk-factor identification and urgent naloxone/ventilatory rescue | Mechanistic review; do not cite as a trial of a specific monitoring strategy |
| **BJA Education TKA review 2026 [6] plus PROSPECT TKA 2022 [7]** | Motor-sparing adductor canal block, surgeon infiltration, non-opioid baseline and planned opioid rescue are central to contemporary knee surgery | Tailor to procedure, patient and rehabilitation capacity; not proof every catheter reduces long-term pain |
| **PROSPECT total hip revision 2026 [8]** | Paracetamol, appropriate NSAID/COX-2, perioperative dexamethasone and selected suprainguinal fascia iliaca/PENG approaches; low-dose IT morphine possible in admitted patients | Hip-specific, not a template for every fracture or day-case procedure |
| **ASRA fifth edition 2025 [9]** | Drug-, dose- and renal-specific neuraxial/deep block/catheter precautions | Intervals and catheter removal require direct current guideline/local assessment; no universal 24-hour rule |
| **ASA/ASRA neuraxial opioid monitoring [10]** | Delayed respiratory depression after single hydrophilic IT opioid means monitoring even without a pump; general adult 24-hour framework | Obstetric low-dose pathways differ by risk and local institutional arrangements |
| **ALLEGRO IV lignocaine [11]** | GI-3 at 72 h: 57.3% lidocaine versus 59.0% placebo; adjusted RR 0.97 (95% CI 0.88–1.07) | Minimally invasive elective colonic surgery; cannot infer no possible effect for every different analgesic endpoint or procedure |
| **IV lignocaine consensus 2021 [12]** | High-risk medicine requiring governance, ideal-body-weight limits, monitoring and separation from local anaesthetic interventions | Safety consensus, not evidence of routine bowel or length-of-stay benefit |
| **International opioid stewardship consensus 2021 [13]** | Avoid routine new MR/transdermal opioids, use function and multimodal care, short discharge supply and planned deprescribing | Patient-specific exceptions for established maintenance therapy require a specialist plan |
| **ASH sickle-cell pain guideline 2020 [15]** | Analgesia within 1 hour, reassess 30–60 min, individual opioid treatment and careful assessment for complications | Individualise for chronic exposure; no routine transfusion for uncomplicated crisis |
| **Saxena et al., BJA Education 2026 [16]** | Differentiates acute amputation pain, stump pain, phantom sensations and PLP; multimodal and MDT strategies | An acute peripheral catheter does not reliably prevent chronic phantom pain |
| **PROSPECT breast update 2026 [17]** | Procedure-specific regional/non-opioid regimens; routine perioperative gabapentin no longer recommended in that setting | Breast-surgery specific; does not forbid every neuropathic-treatment use |
| **Rib-fracture review 2024 [18]** | Effective regional/multimodal analgesia supports inspiration, cough and pulmonary hygiene | Evidence base heterogeneous; avoid blanket mortality claims for any single block |

## 15.1 Interpreting opioid-free anaesthesia claims

- An opioid-free technique may reduce some opioid adverse effects, but **absence of intraoperative opioids does not guarantee superior safety or long-term results**.
- The POFA trial, comparing a dexmedetomidine-based opioid-free approach with remifentanil-based care, was stopped early over a clinically important severe bradycardia signal; interpreting it as proof that all opioid-free regimens are harmful would be equally incorrect.
- An appropriate plan uses adequate local/regional and non-opioid analgesia with a **rescue opioid available** if needed.
- Avoid creating a toxic combination of IV lignocaine and active large-dose local anaesthetic techniques simply to achieve an “opioid-free” label. [13,19]

## 15.2 Prioritised further reading: what to read and why

**Start here:**

- (i) **ANZCA PS41(G) 2023** [2] for clinical governance, informed planning, assessing outcomes and stewardship
- (ii) **PS45 2025** [3] for patient rights, equity and communication
- (iii) **BJA Education, Opioid-induced respiratory depression (Jansen and Dahan, 2024)** [5] for physiology, risk and naloxone
- (iv) **BJA Education, Anaesthesia and analgesia for total knee arthroplasty (de Carvalho et al., July 2026)** [6] for motor-sparing regional and recovery decisions.

**Procedure- and problem-specific:**

- (v) **BJA Education, Pain after lower limb amputation (Saxena et al., March 2026)** [16] for ischaemic/acute/phantom pain mechanisms and long-term support
- (vi) **PROSPECT TKA 2022** [7] and **THA update 2026** [8] for regimen selection and limitations
- (vii) **2025 ASRA antithrombotic fifth edition** [9] for when a catheter can be safely inserted/removed
- (viii) **Foo et al. IV lignocaine consensus** [12] alongside **ALLEGRO** [11], because drug safety and clinical efficacy must be considered together
- (ix) **ASH sickle-cell pain guidance** [15] for a genuinely different acute-pain pathway
- (x) **2024 rib-fracture review** [18] for acute chest-trauma analgesia selection.

**ANZCA Blue Books:**

- The 2017 thoracic epidural and IV lignocaine chapters, 2023 Perioperative management of patients on naltrexone, and 2025 non-obstetric surgery in pregnancy provide useful additional context.
- Older recommendations should be reconciled with newer evidence, particularly ALLEGRO, revised PROSPECT studies and current antithrombotic guidance.
- These notes do not claim a fresh full-text reading of every Blue Book chapter or restricted article.

- Additional verified high-yield sources after the final audit: ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence (fifth edition, 2020) is the broad foundation for pharmacology, assessment, PCA, regional analgesia and special populations [20]; BJA Education, Mehta et al.
- (2023), compares thoracic epidural, paravertebral and plane blocks, useful for the rib-fracture and open thoracic analgesia discussion but extrapolation from surgical thoracotomy to trauma must be acknowledged [21]; PROSPECT appendicectomy recommendations (2024) illustrate how a procedure-specific laparoscopic/open analgesic pathway differs from blanket PCA, gabapentinoid and IV lignocaine prescribing [22].

Additional reading integrated in the final depth pass:

- The Health NZ 2025 national chest injury guideline [23] informs rib-trauma risk stratification and functional escalation.
- NICE sickle-cell acute-pain guidance [24] complements ASH [15] with its more stringent initial analgesia target.
- NICE palliative opioid guidance [25] supports route selection, breakthrough prescriptions and review.

- These sources inform the clinical additions; the exact Set 15 allocation remains the user-supplied workbook.

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
Selected original randomised trials that change how acute-pain techniques are assessed. Interpret their actual populations and endpoints; no trial establishes that one drug or anaesthetic technique is superior in every operation.

| **Trial — original publication** | **Main findings and outcome** | **Exam implication / limitation** |
|---|---|---|
| [ALLEGRO [11] · JAMA 2025](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2827435) | 557 adults analysed after minimally invasive colon surgery: IV lignocaine did not improve GI-3 gut-function recovery at 72 h (57.3% vs 59.0%), or prespecified secondary outcomes. | Do not promise bowel recovery or shortened admission from routine IV lignocaine; distinguish this clinical endpoint from selective analgesic indications and safe infusion governance. |
| [POFA [19] · Anesthesiology 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33630043/) | Dexmedetomidine-based opioid-free anaesthesia versus remifentanil-based balanced anaesthesia: stopped early for five severe-bradycardia cases; adverse-event composite was not improved. | “Opioid-free” is not inherently safer. Specific multimodal co-interventions, protocol and early trial termination constrain extrapolation. |
| [PANSAID · JAMA 2019](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2724188) | 556 patients after hip arthroplasty: paracetamol plus ibuprofen reduced early morphine use versus paracetamol alone; advantage over ibuprofen alone was below the prespecified clinically important difference. | Multimodal addition can produce a small incremental effect. NSAID selection still depends on renal, GI, bleeding and cardiovascular risks. |
| [REGAIN · NEJM 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34623788/) | 1600 older patients undergoing hip-fracture surgery: spinal anaesthesia was not superior to GA for death or inability to walk independently at 60 days (18.5% vs 18.0%). | Choice of anaesthetic should account for patient/procedure and expertise. This is not a trial of every regional analgesic technique or every long-term outcome. |

items.title: Reading list and linked references
items.body:
## Evidence audit and scope

The latest workbook allocates **26 complete outcomes** (12 P1, one P2, five P3, eight P5) and no shared/partial Set 15 rows. The crosswalk points to explanatory teaching—not simply to a question bank. The complete exact workbook wording for each outcome is reproduced in the accompanying audit report.

## Linked references and source register

References are **identified primary professional documents, evidence summaries, articles or original studies**. Date refers to the document/publication, not to a claimed exhaustive literature search.
